_meta.description: Material Knowledge Base for Textile Waste Intelligence Platform - Milestone 3
_meta.purpose: Reference data consumed by Sustainability Intelligence, Environmental Impact, Recycling Recommendation, and Waste Scoring engines.
_meta.disclaimer: Values are approximate reference estimates compiled from general textile LCA (Life Cycle Assessment) literature for academic/internship project use. They are order-of-magnitude representative figures, not laboratory-measured data for any specific product.

units.co2_per_kg: kg CO2-equivalent per kg of fabric produced
units.water_per_kg: liters per kg of fabric produced
units.energy_per_kg: MJ per kg of fabric produced
units.decompose_time_years: approximate natural decomposition time range, in years

_meta.enrichment_note: v1.1 adds material_type, waste_category, common_uses, recommended_actions, scores (0-100 rubric), material_description, sustainability_notes, and recovery_metrics on top of the original v1.0 production-stage LCA fields. All original fields and values are unchanged.

Blended.recycling_method: Requires fiber separation before mechanical or chemical recycling; often downcycled or landfilled otherwise.
Blended.notes: Generic multi-fiber blend; exact composition unknown without lab testing. Apply blend-complexity penalty in scoring engine.
Blended.material_description: Blended fabrics combine two or more fiber types - most often cotton with polyester or elastane - to balance comfort, stretch, and durability. Because different fibers are interwoven, blended textiles are widely used across casualwear and activewear but are harder to recycle cleanly at end of life.
Blended.sustainability_notes: Scores are lower across recyclability and processing feasibility because separating mixed fibers requires specialized (often chemical) technology that isn't widely available yet. Upcycling and donation are prioritized as more practical recovery paths than fiber-level recycling.

Chenille.recycling_method: Textured pile yarn is difficult to mechanically process; industrial recovery or donation preferred.
Chenille.notes: Textured pile-weave fabric, commonly cotton/acrylic/polyester blend, typically used in upholstery/home textiles. Treated as synthetic-blend baseline pending fiber confirmation.
Chenille.material_description: Chenille is a soft, textured pile fabric traditionally used in home furnishings and knitwear, commonly woven from cotton, acrylic, or polyester yarns. Its plush texture comes from tufted yarns that are difficult to separate for conventional recycling.
Chenille.sustainability_notes: The tufted pile construction and typically mixed fiber content bring down recyclability and processing feasibility scores. Environmental benefit is moderate since chenille's blended composition often includes synthetic fibers with meaningful avoided-production impact when diverted from landfill.

Corduroy.recycling_method: Shred and reprocess into new yarn (mechanical recycling).
Corduroy.notes: Heavy cut-pile cotton weave; treated as cotton baseline with slightly higher resource intensity due to fabric weight.
Corduroy.material_description: Corduroy is a durable, ridged cotton fabric known for its distinctive cut-pile 'wale' texture, popular in trousers and outerwear. As a predominantly cotton textile, it shares cotton's strong natural-fiber recycling profile.
Corduroy.sustainability_notes: High recyclability and processing feasibility reflect its cotton base and established mechanical recycling pathways. The heavier fabric weight slightly increases production resource intensity compared to plain cotton, giving it a solid environmental benefit score.

Cotton.recycling_method: Shred and reprocess into new yarn (mechanical recycling).
Cotton.notes: Natural fiber, compostable in undyed/untreated form.
Cotton.material_description: Cotton is one of the most widely used natural fibers in the world, valued for its softness, breathability, and versatility across garments and home textiles. It has a mature, well-established recycling and reuse ecosystem.
Cotton.sustainability_notes: Cotton scores high across all four metrics due to its natural biodegradability, established mechanical recycling infrastructure, and strong secondhand market. Its main environmental cost is high water usage during cultivation, which recovery pathways help offset.

Crepe.recycling_method: Fiber-dependent; treat as synthetic baseline unless fiber composition is separately confirmed.
Crepe.notes: Crinkled weave fabric commonly made from polyester, silk, or wool; treated as synthetic baseline pending fiber confirmation.
Crepe.material_description: Crepe refers to a distinctively crinkled weave rather than a single fiber type, commonly produced from polyester, silk, or wool yarns. This ambiguity in fiber origin makes standardized recycling difficult.
Crepe.sustainability_notes: Scores assume a synthetic (polyester-like) baseline given prevalence in ready-to-wear garments. Recyclability and processing feasibility are limited by the weave's fiber ambiguity; reuse and upcycling are the more realistic recovery routes.

Denim.recycling_method: Shred into fiber for insulation, new denim blends, or industrial recovery.
Denim.notes: Heavy cotton twill; classic denim manufacturing is highly water-intensive. Stretch denim (with elastane) reduces recyclability.
Denim.material_description: Denim is a rugged cotton twill fabric best known for jeans and casualwear, often blended with a small amount of elastane for stretch. It has one of the strongest secondhand markets of any textile.
Denim.sustainability_notes: Denim scores well on reuse and recyclability thanks to its cotton base and thriving resale culture, though stretch-denim blends and heavy dyeing slightly reduce processing ease. Its high water footprint during production makes recovery especially valuable environmentally.

Fleece.recycling_method: Shred → pellet → respin (mechanical) or chemical depolymerization.
Fleece.notes: Synthetic polyester knit pile; known microplastic-shedding risk during washing.
Fleece.material_description: Fleece is a soft, insulating knit fabric made primarily from polyester, widely used in jackets, blankets, and cold-weather apparel. It benefits from established synthetic-fiber recycling infrastructure.
Fleece.sustainability_notes: As a polyester-based textile, fleece scores reasonably well on recyclability and environmental benefit due to mature mechanical and chemical recycling routes for polyester. Microfiber shedding during washing is a known environmental concern not fully captured in these production-stage metrics.

Leather.recycling_method: Rarely recycled at fiber level; upcycling into smaller leather goods or industrial recovery preferred. May require hazardous-waste handling due to tanning chemicals.
Leather.notes: Chrome-tanned leather; very high environmental footprint from livestock farming and tanning chemicals. Often falls under Hazardous Textile Waste category due to chromium content.
Leather.material_description: Leather is an animal-hide material valued for its durability and premium feel, used in jackets, bags, shoes, and upholstery. Its production and disposal both carry significant environmental and chemical-handling considerations.
Leather.sustainability_notes: Leather scores very low on recyclability and processing feasibility because chrome-tanning chemicals complicate standard textile recycling and can require hazardous-waste handling. Its environmental benefit score is high specifically because leather production has one of the largest per-kg footprints of any material here, making diversion from landfill especially impactful.

Linen.recycling_method: Shred and reprocess into new yarn (mechanical recycling).
Linen.notes: Flax-based natural fiber; one of the lowest-impact natural textiles.
Linen.material_description: Linen is a natural fiber made from the flax plant, prized for its breathability and low environmental footprint. It is among the most sustainable natural fibers used in textiles today.
Linen.sustainability_notes: Linen scores very high on recyclability and processing feasibility thanks to its natural, single-fiber composition and low-impact cultivation. Its environmental benefit score is comparatively moderate simply because its original production footprint is already low, leaving less impact to 'save' through recovery.

Nylon.recycling_method: Chemical depolymerization (e.g., regenerated nylon processes) or mechanical regrind.
Nylon.notes: Petroleum-based synthetic; chemical recycling routes increasingly available for post-consumer nylon.
Nylon.material_description: Nylon is a durable, petroleum-based synthetic fiber commonly used in activewear, hosiery, and outerwear shells. Chemical recycling technologies for nylon are emerging but not yet as widespread as those for polyester.
Nylon.sustainability_notes: Moderate scores reflect nylon's growing but still-limited chemical recycling infrastructure. Its high production energy intensity gives it a solid environmental benefit score when successfully diverted from landfill and recycled.

Polyester.recycling_method: Shred → pellet → respin (mechanical, e.g. rPET) or chemical depolymerization.
Polyester.notes: Most common synthetic fiber; widely recyclable via mechanical or chemical routes.
Polyester.material_description: Polyester is the most widely produced synthetic textile fiber globally, used across apparel, activewear, and upholstery. It has one of the most mature recycling ecosystems among synthetic fibers, including mechanical (rPET) and chemical routes.
Polyester.sustainability_notes: Polyester scores well on recyclability and processing feasibility due to established rPET recycling infrastructure. Its high production energy footprint translates into a strong environmental benefit score when recycled rather than landfilled.

Satin.recycling_method: Fiber-dependent; treat as synthetic (polyester-based) baseline unless confirmed otherwise.
Satin.notes: Glossy weave commonly made from polyester or silk; treated as synthetic baseline pending fiber confirmation.
Satin.material_description: Satin describes a glossy weave structure rather than a single fiber, typically produced from polyester or silk yarns for eveningwear, linings, and bridalwear. Its fiber ambiguity limits standardized recycling.
Satin.sustainability_notes: Scores assume a synthetic (polyester-like) baseline given common usage in fast-fashion eveningwear. Limited recyclability and processing feasibility reflect the difficulty of confirming exact fiber content without lab testing; upcycling and donation are the more practical recovery paths.

Silk.recycling_method: Rarely mechanically recycled; reuse, resale, and donation are the primary recovery pathways.
Silk.notes: Natural protein fiber; resource-intensive sericulture process (mulberry cultivation and silkworm rearing).
Silk.material_description: Silk is a luxurious natural protein fiber produced by silkworms, used in scarves, blouses, and eveningwear. It carries a resource-intensive production process but a strong secondhand and resale market.
Silk.sustainability_notes: Silk scores low on recyclability and processing feasibility since it is rarely mechanically recycled at scale, but scores high on reuse given its durability and enduring resale value. Its environmental benefit reflects the meaningful resource cost of sericulture that reuse and donation help offset.

Terrycloth.recycling_method: Shred and reprocess into new yarn (mechanical recycling).
Terrycloth.notes: Absorbent cotton loop-pile fabric (toweling); treated as cotton baseline.
Terrycloth.material_description: Terrycloth is an absorbent, looped-pile cotton fabric best known for towels and bathrobes. As a cotton-based textile, it shares cotton's strong recyclability profile, often finding a second life as industrial wiping cloths.
Terrycloth.sustainability_notes: High recyclability and processing feasibility scores reflect its cotton composition and the well-established practice of converting worn towels into industrial rags or recycled fiber. Its environmental benefit score tracks closely with cotton given similar water-intensive production.

Unclassified.recycling_method: Manual inspection required - classification confidence too low for an automated recommendation.
Unclassified.notes: Classifier confidence too low to assign a fabric type. Downstream engines should flag this item for manual review rather than generating a sustainability/recycling score.
common_uses: Unknown - insufficient visual confidence for classification
Unclassified.material_description: This item could not be confidently matched to a known fabric class by the classification model. Sustainability and recycling recommendations cannot be reliably generated without further inspection.
Unclassified.sustainability_notes: All quantitative scores are intentionally left unset (null) because assigning a numeric sustainability score to an unknown material would be misleading. Items in this category should be flagged for manual review rather than processed through the automated sustainability pipeline.

Viscose.recycling_method: Emerging closed-loop chemical recycling (Lyocell-style processes); otherwise compostable.
Viscose.notes: Semi-synthetic cellulose fiber (rayon); biodegradable but manufacturing involves intensive chemical processing.
Viscose.material_description: Viscose (rayon) is a semi-synthetic cellulose fiber derived from wood pulp, offering a silk-like drape at a lower cost. It is biodegradable but involves chemically intensive processing during manufacturing.
Viscose.sustainability_notes: Moderate scores reflect viscose's biodegradable cellulose base offset by limited, still-emerging closed-loop chemical recycling infrastructure. Its environmental benefit score accounts for the meaningful chemical processing footprint involved in production.

Wool.recycling_method: Shredded and re-carded into new wool fiber.
Wool.notes: Natural protein fiber from livestock; high production footprint (methane) but excellent mechanical recyclability and biodegradability.
Wool.material_description: Wool is a natural protein fiber sheared from sheep, valued for its warmth, durability, and biodegradability, commonly used in sweaters, coats, and blankets. It has a long-established mechanical recycling tradition (sometimes called 'wool shoddy').
Wool.sustainability_notes: Wool scores well on recyclability, reuse, and processing feasibility thanks to a mature mechanical recycling industry and durable, mendable garments. Its environmental benefit score is high because wool production carries a notably large footprint (largely methane from livestock), making recovery especially valuable.
